metamorphosis

/met-uh-MOR-fuh-sis/ - the stress falls on MOR · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Metamorphosis means a complete change of form or character.

Friends from her quiet suburb barely recognized the woman on stage; the metamorphosis from shy bookkeeper to headlining comic had taken six years of open mics.

Example

The novel traces one man's metamorphosis: the timid clerk of chapter one, who apologizes to furniture, ends the book running a smuggling ring with perfect calm, and the author makes every step of the change believable.

Metamorphosis is total — form or character rebuilt, not refreshed. A pruned rosebush is a change; the vacant lot that five years of planting turned into a shaded orchard walk has undergone metamorphosis. Reach for the word only when the before and after barely share a skeleton.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

overhaul: An overhaul is a thorough, deliberate rebuild — an engine or a curriculum taken apart and put back better — that stops short of changing what the thing is. A metamorphosis crosses that line: after it, the before and after barely share a skeleton.

rebirth: A rebirth is a fresh start — the emphasis is renewal, a thing alive again, more than any change in what it looks like or is. Metamorphosis stresses altered form: the shape or character has been rebuilt so completely that the original is hard to find.

reinvention: Reinvention is what people, brands, and careers do to themselves on purpose — a deliberate remaking of image or direction. A metamorphosis needs no intent and no self: a landscape, an institution, or a timid clerk can undergo one, and the word measures the astonishing distance crossed.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

stasis: a state in which nothing moves or changes at all

continuity: an unbroken carrying-on of the same form

Where it sits · how deep the change goes

adjustment → makeover → metamorphosis

adjustment vs. metamorphosis: An adjustment is far milder than a metamorphosis — a nudge to one setting, with the thing itself left untouched.

makeover vs. metamorphosis: A makeover is milder than a metamorphosis — it freshens the surface, while a metamorphosis rebuilds the creature underneath.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — meta-: change, beyond (Greek)

Root — morph: form, shape (Greek morphe)

Suffix — -osis: a process or condition

Put it together: Meta- (change) + morph (form) + -osis (a process) = the process of changing form. Greek used metamorphosis for gods swapping shapes; biology borrowed it for the caterpillar's rebuild, and everyday English for any change so complete that the old form is gone.

Use the root in a new word: morph: Film students don't get to try the morph effect until the third week of class.

Root Check

Word Choice

formal / literary

Metamorphosis is a grand word, and it should be spent on grand changes — a life, an institution, an art form rebuilt beyond recognition. For ordinary improvement, overhaul or makeover is honest; and where this unit's transmute stresses one substance turned into another, metamorphosis stresses the astonishing distance between before and after.
